summary: Describes how SNMP messages are dispatched to the proper message processing models, and requests to SNMP applications. It also describes the SNMPv3 message processing model. It replaces RFC 2262 and was replaced by RFC 2572.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the sorting room that sends each network-manager message to the right place, updated from an earlier version and later replaced.

questions: how does snmp route messages to applications
how does snmpv3 message processing work
subtitle: How SNMP engines route messages to the right handlers and security subsystems

tldr.problem: SNMP needs to support multiple message format versions (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, SNMPv3) and route them to appropriate applications while coordinating security processing.
tldr.mechanism: A Dispatcher component routes incoming messages to version-specific Message Processing Models, which extract the message components and work with the Security Subsystem, then dispatches PDUs to the correct applications based on context and PDU type.
tldr.outcome: SNMP engines can transparently handle multiple protocol versions and apply appropriate security without each application needing to know the version details, though it replaced RFC 2262 and was later superseded.

today: RFC 2272 defined SNMPv3 message processing and was made obsolete by RFC 2572. The specification remains foundational to understanding how modern SNMP engines route and secure network management traffic.

sections.title: SNMP Message Processing Architecture
sections.content: The SNMP architecture [RFC 2271] divides an SNMP engine into four major components: a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem, and an Access Control Subsystem. RFC 2272 describes how the Dispatcher and Message Processing Subsystem work together to handle SNMP messages. A Message Processing Model is responsible for understanding a specific version of SNMP messages, extracting the protocol data unit (PDU) from the message, and coordinating with the Security Subsystem to validate or apply security. The Dispatcher is the central hub that sends and receives all messages and routes PDUs to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: An SNMP engine has a central router (the Dispatcher) that takes in messages, checks what version they are, passes them to version-specific handlers, and sends the contents to the right application.

sections.title: The Dispatcher and Message Processing Models
sections.content:
The Dispatcher is the core component: there is exactly one per SNMP engine. For outgoing messages, an application gives the Dispatcher a PDU and specifies which Message Processing Model (version) to use. The Dispatcher calls that model to prepare the message, apply security, and send it over the network.

For incoming messages, the Dispatcher examines the message, determines its version, and passes it to the matching Message Processing Model to extract the PDU and apply security validation. The Message Processing Subsystem can support multiple models at once: currently SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3, though only SNMPv3 is described in this RFC. Each model converts between the network message format and a generic internal format that applications can use, regardless of the original version.
sections.plainLanguage: The Dispatcher is like a mail sorter. When a message comes in, it reads the version number and hands it to the right handler. When an app wants to send a message, the sorter picks the version handler the app asked for.

sections.title: SNMPv3 Message Structure
sections.content:
An SNMPv3 message consists of a message version field (set to 3), global administrative data (including message ID, maximum message size, and security flags), security model-specific parameters, and the scoped PDU data. The message ID coordinates request-response pairs and helps prevent replay attacks. The msgMaxSize field tells the receiver the largest message the sender can accept.

The msgFlags field contains three bits: the authFlag indicates whether the message is authenticated, the privFlag indicates whether the data is encrypted, and the reportableFlag indicates whether the receiver should send a Report PDU if processing fails. These three flags together define the security level: no authentication and no privacy, authentication but no privacy, or authentication with privacy. Privacy requires authentication; authentication alone is valid, but privacy without authentication is not permitted.

The scoped PDU data may be plaintext or encrypted. A scoped PDU contains a context engine ID (identifying which SNMP engine the data is from or for), a context name (identifying a management context), and the actual PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: An SNMPv3 message has a header with a version number, an ID, size limit, security flags, and either plaintext or encrypted management data inside.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Messages
sections.content:
When an application wants to send a message, it calls the Dispatcher with a PDU, target address, security model, and security parameters. The Dispatcher generates a unique handle for tracking, then calls the appropriate Message Processing Model's prepare function, passing all the application-provided data. The model calls the Security Subsystem to apply security, returns the complete message, and the Dispatcher sends it over the network.

When a message arrives, the Dispatcher increments a statistics counter, checks that the message can be parsed, determines the version, and passes the message to the matching Message Processing Model. The model calls the Security Subsystem to validate security and extract the PDU. The Dispatcher then determines which application should handle the PDU based on context engine ID and PDU type. If an application has registered for that combination, the PDU is dispatched to it. If no application is registered, an error counter is incremented and an error response may be sent.

Responses follow a similar path: the application calls returnResponsePDU with the response PDU and the state reference from the original request. The Dispatcher passes it to the Message Processing Model, which applies security and returns the message, then sends it back to the requester.
sections.plainLanguage: To send a message, the app gives the Dispatcher a PDU and the destination; the Dispatcher hands it to the version handler, which applies security and sends it. For incoming messages, the Dispatcher checks the version, passes it to the handler, checks which app registered for that type, and delivers it.

sections.title: Application Registration and State Management
sections.content:
Applications that want to receive PDUs of a particular type must register with the Dispatcher, specifying the context engine ID and PDU type combination they handle. The combination must be registered only once; if another application has already claimed it, the registration fails. Each application stores state information associated with outgoing requests so that incoming responses can be matched to the right application using the sendPduHandle.

The Message Processing Model maintains the abstract data elements needed to process messages: messageProcessingModel (the version), securityModel, securityName (the security principal), securityLevel, contextEngineID, contextName, pduVersion, and the PDU itself. These are extracted from incoming messages or provided by applications for outgoing messages. The Dispatcher also collects statistics such as counters for unknown security models, invalid messages, and unregistered PDU handlers, making them accessible to remote management via MIB objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications register by saying 'I will handle Get requests for this context', and the Dispatcher remembers that. The Dispatcher also tracks request IDs so responses reach the right application and counts errors for monitoring.
